rv.q: It's an evening that, frankly, gets everything right.
And it’s all totally, soul-feedingly wonderful.

Through Canadian folk tunes and simple storytelling, they’ve created something incredibly pure, life-affirming and human – it’s the best tonic there can be to a world that feels so divided at the moment.
The production embodies a spirit of communal endeavour that is badly needed at the moment.
Even so, this is a moving, irresistible show that unapologetically champions kindness.
For all its craft, there are moments when Come From Away feels like an advertisement for Canadian decency and its capacity to improve the lives of malcontent Americans.
My misgivings on that front haven’t entirely receded.
It’s stirring and a bit queasy-making.
There's a lot to love about Come from Away, the feelgood 9/11 musical, if you allow yourself to go with the flow of slightly hokey camaraderie.
The show could hardly be better done even if, as a work of art, I found it lacking in complexity and argument.
Come from Away sticks resolutely to a much nicer world, without conflict, and without much drama either.
This feel-good show about a feel-bad world-shattering event is also a little show with a big heart.
Come From Away is this year's must-see musical.
Hope, resilience, community, trust, generosity and love, Come From Away is a musical theatre production for our times.
Most importantly of all, it has a feelgood factor that simply doesn't let-up.
Come from near, come from far, come from away - just make sure you come and see this show.
Come From Away is laugh-out-loud funny, emotional, and a true showcase of the strength of humanity.

cn.t: Critics embrace this heartwarming musical about Gander's 9/11 hospitality as an uplifting tonic, praising its folksy charm and nimble staging, though some find its relentless celebration of kindness overly earnest and bludgeoning.

vr.q: the pace is tremendous... the ending which is akin to a hoedown is entertaining and hugely uplifting
